extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and other practitioners who represent clients (particularly foreign-domiciled trademark applicants) before the USPTO
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and obligations governing competent, diligent, and candid practice before the USPTO (especially in trademark matters), including signature, certification, supervision, client-communication, and reinstatement/monitoring requirements following discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Counsel Rule (requirement for U.S.-licensed attorney)
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign-domiciled trademark applicants or registrants must be represented before the USPTO by an attorney who is licensed to practice law in the United States (37 C.F.R. § 2.11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy objective: instill public confidence that U.S. registrations issued to foreign applicants are not subject to invalidation for reasons such as improper signatures; ensure foreign applicants are assisted only by authorized practitioners subject to USPTO disciplinary rules. See 84 Fed. Reg. 31498 (Final Rule) and TMEP § 601.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification requirements when presenting documents to the USPTO (37 C.F.R. § 11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: By presenting a document to the USPTO, the presenter certifies that statements made on the presenter's own knowledge are true and statements made on information and belief are believed to be true, and that the filing meets the § 11.18(b)(2) requirements (reasonable inquiry, not for improper purpose, legal contentions warranted, factual contentions have evidentiary support, denials warranted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key elements: (b)(1) truthfulness of statements; (b)(2) certification that, after inquiry reasonable under the circumstances, (i) paper not presented for improper purpose; (ii) legal contentions warranted by existing law or a nonfrivolous argument; (iii) factual contentions have evidentiary support or are likely to after investigation; (iv) denials are warranted. Violations may jeopardize the probative value of the filing and may expose signatories to criminal penalties (e.g., 18 U.S.C. § 1001).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark application declaration factual assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Declarations in trademark applications (use-based under 15 U.S.C. § 1051(a)) contain specific factual assertions to which § 11.18 certifications apply: signatory believes applicant is owner; mark is in use in commerce as of filing date for listed goods/services; specimen shows the mark as used on or in connection with the goods/services as of filing date; facts recited are accurate to the best of the signatory's knowledge and belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factual assertions are made under penalty of perjury; knowingly false statements subject to criminal penalty. Presenters must have a reasonable inquiry supporting these factual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark signature rules (37 C.F.R. § 2.193 and related provisions; TMEP § 611.01(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: All signatures must be personally entered by the named signatory; a person electronically signing via TEAS must personally enter any adopted signature placed between two forward slash ('/') symbols in the signature block on the electronic submission (37 C.F.R. § 2.193(a),(c); § 11.15(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proscription: a person may not delegate authority to sign, no person may sign or enter the name of another, typing another's electronic signature is not a valid signature, and use of document-signing software to create someone else's signature is not permitted. TMEP § 611.01(c) provides explicit examples and sanctions for violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to review and ensure accuracy of signature information on filings
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Signature Information' on submission forms must correctly identify the named signatory (not the attorney when another person actually signed); practitioners must identify and correct recurring or obvious signature errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated failure to identify an obvious recurring error in filings (e.g., misidentifying signatory name) indicates lack of care and attention; such failures may cause actual or potential harm to clients' IP rights and adversely affect USPTO processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must provide competent representation, which includes understanding USPTO signature rules and guidance, presenting documents signed in accordance with those rules, adequately reviewing specimens and filings, and supporting factual assertions in declarations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of incompetence: not understanding signature rules; impermissibly entering clients' signatures; presenting declarations that do not support asserted facts; filing many documents containing obvious errors. Competence is assessed by the practitioner's knowledge and the care exercised in filings and supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must act with reasonable diligence in representing clients, including understanding applicable USPTO rules, ensuring filings comply with signature and certification rules, adequately reviewing filings and specimens, and timely informing relevant USPTO offices when problems arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to act diligently (e.g., filing improperly signed documents, inadequate review of many submissions) is a basis for discipline and may be treated together with competency failings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client communication duties (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(2) and (a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must inform affected clients of actual or potential harm to their pending applications or issued registrations, keep clients reasonably informed of the status of their matters, and explain matters sufficiently to permit informed decisions (including opting for alternate counsel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to notify clients about actual or potential harms arising from rule violations (e.g., signature-rule violations) is a violation of client-communication obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of candor to the tribunal/USPTO (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1),(a)(3),(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must be candid with the USPTO and timely report material matters to the Office (e.g., promptly notifying the Office of the Deputy Commissioner for Trademark Examination Policy of violations and providing lists of improperly signed documents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay or material misrepresentations to the Office (including false statements in communications about who signed documents) violate the duty of candor and may result in discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a violation to present trademark documents to the USPTO that the practitioner knows were not signed by the named signatory, or to provide inaccurate information to USPTO officials about such violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include falsely stating 'never allowed anyone else to sign his name' when records show paralegal or others entered signatures; such misrepresentations support disciplinary sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engaging in conduct prejudicial to the administration of the USPTO trademark system (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner conduct that adversely affects the integrity of USPTO registration and maintenance processes—such as filing improperly signed documents, failing to adequately review specimens, not conducting a reasonable inquiry under § 11.18, or not timely informing the USPTO—constitutes prejudicial conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative list of prejudicial acts: not understanding signature rules, impermissibly entering client signatures on many documents, filing declarations unsupported by facts, failing adequate review resulting in thousands of filings with obvious errors, and failing to timely notify the Office of such problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to supervise non-attorneys and review assistants' work
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners who rely on paralegals or assistants must adequately supervise them and ensure filings made on clients' behalf comply with USPTO signature and certification rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to supervise (e.g., a paralegal entering signatures or filing without practitioner knowledge) supports findings of incompetence/diligence violations and can cause client harm and discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and remediation conditions after discipline (suspension, probation, limited recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary sanctions may include suspension from practice, limited recognition to close client matters, a probationary period with specific conditions, and obligations to pay disciplinary costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific conditions may include: six-month suspension; 30-day limited recognition to conclude matters; compliance with 37 C.F.R. § 11.58; 12-month probation after petition for reinstatement; payment of costs per 37 C.F.R. § 11.60(d)(2); waiver of appeal rights as part of settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement prerequisites and remedial education
rubrics_metrics.description: Before reinstatement, a disciplined practitioner may be required to complete specified education and attestations, such as completing USPTO's Trademark Basics Boot Camp modules, thoroughly reviewing the TMEP (including signature provisions), and completing continuing legal education in ethics/professional responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent must provide written declarations under 28 U.S.C. § 1746 confirming completion of eight Boot Camp modules, a thorough review of the TMEP, and two hours of CLE in ethics prior to reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring, audits, and practice monitors during probation
rubrics_metrics.description: Probation may require appointment of a Patent Practice Monitor and a Trademark Practice Monitor who meet qualifications (registered/authorized, active registration, 5 years continuous practice) to audit filings, review processes, and submit quarterly reports to OED verifying compliance with MPEP/TMEP and timely client communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitors must: conduct an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances including audits; identify specific filings that represent significant problems; make recommendations to improve procedures; submit initial reports within 91 days of reinstatement and then every 90 days; maintain confidentiality per 37 C.F.R. § 11.106. Practitioner is responsible for finding and paying monitors and ensuring timely submission of reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ongoing account/search and notification obligations during suspension/probation
rubrics_metrics.description: During suspension and probation, practitioners may be barred from accessing/using USPTO.gov accounts and must perform regular searches of USPTO public systems for filings that improperly identify them as attorney of record and promptly notify the appropriate USPTO offices if such filings are found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific obligations: do bi-weekly searches of the USPTO trademark search system for filings that identify the practitioner as attorney of record and were filed without their knowledge/consent (during limited recognition and until reinstatement); bi-weekly searches of publicly available patent records for the same; submit written reports to OED every two months confirming searches and any notifications sent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification violations jeopardize probative value and carry potential criminal exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of certification obligations (e.g., false statements under § 11.18 and declarations under penalty of perjury) may jeopardize the probative value of filings and can expose the signatory to criminal penalties (18 U.S.C. § 1001 and other statutes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must conduct reasonable inquiry into facts supporting filings; failure to do so undermines the filing's evidentiary weight and may trigger both disciplinary and criminal consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: TMEP and USPTO published guidance are readily available and practitioners expected to know them
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO regularly publishes and updates the Trademark Manual of Examining Procedure and other guidance (TMEP, Federal Register notices, USPTO trademark webpage), and practitioners who represent trademark clients are reasonably expected to know applicable rules and guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: TMEP § 611.01(c) (signature rules) and TMEP § 601 (U.S. Counsel Rule). Prior disciplinary decisions and agency webpages are public resources practitioners should consult; ignorance of published guidance is not a defense to misconduct findings.
